Do AI Models Learn Like Humans?

Sometimes: sense-specific world models raised on infant-like input reproduce some signatures of early development and miss others

Somesh Mohapatra

Independent · 15 October 2026

Infants learn a model of their world from a modest amount of experience that arrives once, in order, through senses that start immature and mature on different clocks. Whether these constraints matter for machine learning is usually assumed rather than tested. Here we build the smallest system that can test them: one predictive world model per sense (vision, hearing, touch and proprioception) in a synthetic multisensory nursery, each fed through an age-indexed model of sensory immaturity and read out at checkpoints standing for 0, 3, 6 and 12 months, plus a fusion world model that combines them. Six training regimes separate the input schedule, network growth and data order. The input schedule alone reproduces the infant order of sensory maturation, but learning lags well behind what the input allows: at the newborn checkpoint the vision model’s toy-position read-out is R² = 0.02, although a supervised network extracts 0.59 from the same input. Growing the network halves training compute and slows learning. Early immaturity improves hearing on clean input (R² 0.45 ± 0.01 versus 0.37 ± 0.04) at a small cost in vision. Fusing the senses tracks a fully hidden toy better than any one sense (R² 0.77 ± 0.06 versus 0.64 ± 0.09 for vision memory). But no model expects a hidden toy to persist: the fused model’s apparent surprise disappears when hearing is prevented from giving the event away. In these synthetic models, infant-like input is therefore sufficient for infant-like trajectories of what is decodable, but not for infant-like expectations about hidden objects.

Introduction

By their first birthday, infants expect hidden objects to persist and unsupported objects to fall, attribute goals to agents, and have tuned their perception to the faces and speech sounds around them (Spelke and Kinzler 2007; Baillargeon, Spelke, and Wasserman 1985; Werker and Tees 1984; Pascalis, Haan, and Nelson 2002). They achieve this from a few thousand waking hours of egocentric, repetitive experience that arrives once and in order (Smith et al. 2018). Self-supervised networks trained on a single child’s headcam footage now learn useful visual representations and word meanings (Orhan, Gupta, and Lake 2020; Orhan and Lake 2024; Vong et al. 2024), and expectations about intuitive physics can emerge from video prediction alone (Garrido et al. 2025). The question this raises is not whether machines can learn from infant data, but whether the way infants receive their data matters for what is learned.

Infant learning differs from standard training in four documented ways. The senses start immature: newborn acuity is about 1 cycle per degree and contrast sensitivity is a small fraction of the adult’s (Banks and Bennett 1988; Norcia and Tyler 1985). They come online in a fixed order, with touch first, hearing before birth and vision at birth, and this staggered onset may limit competition between the senses (Turkewitz and Kenny 1982). Plasticity is staggered across senses and levels of the hierarchy (Hensch 2005; Werker and Hensch 2015), and the cortex overproduces synapses and then prunes them rather than adding neurons (Huttenlocher and Dabholkar 1997). And experience is a single non-stationary stream (Smith et al. 2018). In networks, initially blurred or achromatic input can make recognition more robust (L. Vogelsang et al. 2018; M. Vogelsang et al. 2024), slowly changing infant video helps self-supervised learning (Sheybani et al. 2023), and deep networks show their own critical periods, including for multisensory integration (Achille, Rovere, and Soatto 2017; Kleinman, Achille, and Soatto 2023). Yet the benefit of “starting small” (Elman 1993) was challenged by later simulations (Rohde and Plaut 1999), curricula help little on standard benchmarks and mainly under limited training budgets or noisy labels (Wu, Dyer, and Neyshabur 2021), and stage-like learning can arise from learning dynamics alone (Saxe, McClelland, and Ganguli 2019).

We therefore treat developmental constraints as hypotheses to test rather than design choices to assume. Nothing in our models is gated by age: no module switches on at a given month, and every capability is measured. We ask four questions, each answered in one section of Results. Do senses mature in the infant order, and is that a property of learning or of the input? Does starting with immature input help? Do combined senses keep information that each sense loses? And do models that can decode a hidden object also expect it to persist?

Results

A testbed of sense-specific developmental world models

The nursery (Fig. 1a; Methods) renders one toy of four types, a babbling hand and, in half the scenes, a vertical screen into four streams: 32×32 colour vision, binaural hearing (2 ears × 32 frequency bins, panned by position and passing through the screen), an 8×8 tactile patch on the hand, and four-dimensional proprioception. Each toy type is specified redundantly across senses, by shape and colour, pitch, and felt shape (Bahrick and Lickliter 2000).

Each sense is filtered by a fixed front end whose parameters follow the age aa (Fig. 1b, c; Table 1). For vision we use published infant acuity and contrast sensitivity (Norcia and Tyler 1985; Banks and Bennett 1988); for hearing, touch and proprioception we use coarse placeholder tables that respect the known order of maturation. Behind each front end is a world model of the same family (Methods): an encoder, a residual dynamics model over a memory window, and a decoder, trained to reconstruct the current observation and predict the next one. Each sense is trained in one continuous run of four stages and read out at the end of each stage; we call these checkpoints 0, 3, 6 and 12 months. Six regimes (Fig. 1d; Table 2) cross two levers, the input schedule and network growth, with two order controls. All regimes see the same data for the same number of updates.

The input schedule sets the order; learning lags the input

With immature input, the vision model cannot localise the toy at the first two checkpoints (position R² 0.02 ± 0.00 and 0.36 ± 0.10) and then rises steeply to 0.86 ± 0.04 (Fig. 2a). The same network trained on adult-quality input localises the toy from the first checkpoint (0.71 ± 0.02) and ends at 0.90 ± 0.02. Hearing rises modestly as binaural cues mature, and proprioception and touch are near their final level throughout (Fig. 2c, e). The infant order of maturation, body senses first, hearing next, vision last, therefore appears; half-ceiling ages are touch 0, hearing 4 and vision 0 months (Kendall τ = 0.00 against the infant order; Fig. 2f). This agreement is put there by the front-end tables and is not a finding about learning.

Two controls separate learning from input. First, probing on adult-quality input asks a model trained on blurred images to generalise to sharp ones. Probing instead on each checkpoint’s own input (Fig. 2b) gives 0.00 ± 0.01 at 0 months and 0.86 ± 0.04 at 12, so the early failure is not a distribution-shift artefact. Second, the newborn input is not empty: a supervised network trained directly on it decodes toy position with R² = 0.59, rising to 0.95 at 12 months (Fig. 2a, dashed). The self-supervised vision model reaches only a small fraction of what its input allows at the early checkpoints and closes the gap later (Fig. 2d). The infant-like curve is thus a joint product of what the input contains and how slowly a predictive objective extracts a small object from a blurred, low-contrast scene.

Growth slows learning and halves compute

Adding growth to immature input does not change the shape of the curve; it delays it (Fig. 2a). The grown vision model is still at R² 0.04 ± 0.02 at the 3-month checkpoint and ends at 0.80 ± 0.08, against 0.86 ± 0.04 for the fixed-size network; identity accuracy is 0.50 ± 0.08 against 0.67 ± 0.04 (Hedges’ g = −2.2, p = 0.05). Growth without immature input learns quickly and ends near the adult-input model (0.88 ± 0.03). At matched updates, growing networks use 0.48 of the fixed network’s parameter-updates (Fig. 3d). The delay has a simple cause (Box 1): units added with zero outgoing weights receive zero gradient on their incoming weights until the outgoing weights move, so new capacity contributes nothing at first.

Early immaturity: a small cost in vision, a benefit in hearing

On clean input the adult-input vision model is best. Immature input costs 0.90 − 0.86 in R² (g = −1.0, p = 0.21). Tested on newborn-quality input, every model fails (Fig. 3a), with regimes that saw immature input failing less on average (−0.24 ± 0.10 against −0.40 ± 0.30 for adult input), but the difference is within seed variability (p = 0.46). We do not claim a robustness benefit in vision.

Hearing is different. Models that heard immature sound early localise better on clean input at 12 months (0.45 ± 0.01 immature, 0.47 ± 0.01 immature with growth) than models that only heard adult-quality sound (0.37 ± 0.04 adult input, 0.27 ± 0.12 growth only; Fig. 3b; g = 2.3, p = 0.06). Shuffled input quality (0.43) is close to the immature schedule, which suggests that the benefit comes from having heard degraded input at all, a form of augmentation, more than from its order. Reversing the schedule is the clearest negative control: the vision model that ends on newborn-quality input falls from 0.88 to 0.67.

Combined senses keep what each sense loses

During a long occlusion, the hidden toy’s horizontal position can be decoded from the vision model’s memory (R² 0.64 ± 0.09 at 12 months), from hearing, which passes through the screen (0.48 ± 0.05), and best from the fused world model (0.77 ± 0.06; Fig. 4a; paired difference fused minus vision positive in every seed). The advantage appears at 6 months and nothing is decodable at 0 to 3 months, when neither vision nor binaural hearing can localise. For a visible toy, the fused state is better than vision alone (0.88 ± 0.04 against 0.80 ± 0.08) and, with vision switched off, still recovers position from hearing, touch and the hand (0.53 ± 0.01; Fig. 4b).

Decodable is not expected

No unimodal vision model, in any regime, has a positive VoE index (Fig. 4c): all are more surprised when the toy reappears than when it fails to, like a predictor that copies the last frame (Fig. 4e). This holds although the hidden toy’s position is decodable from the same model’s memory. Squared-error prediction explains it (Box 1): the error-minimising forecast is the conditional mean of the next frame, and when the reappearance time is uncertain that mean is dominated by the screen.

The fused model does show a positive index when the toy vanishes from every sense (0.30 ± 0.10 at 12 months), but its channels show where the surprise comes from: hearing 0.75 ± 0.06, vision −0.09 ± 0.02 (Fig. 4d). The model notices that the sound stopped. When the toy vanishes from sight but keeps sounding, the overall index is −0.01 ± 0.01 and the vision channel −0.08 ± 0.09; when a silent toy vanishes, they are −0.05 ± 0.02 and −0.30 ± 0.09. Without a sound to give the event away, the fused model does not expect the toy back either. A read-out can show that information about a hidden object is present while the model’s predictions do not use it; object permanence has to be tested with paradigms, not probes.

Convergent evidence from two companion studies

Two companion studies with independent code and stimuli point the same way (Fig. 5). In compact networks on a shape-versus-texture task, the acuity schedule alone produced an infant-like curve whatever the capacity strategy, growing networks were slowest, and the same three months of blur caused a lasting deficit only when they came first: a critical period in a plain continuous run with no plasticity schedule, in line with critical periods reported in deep networks (Achille, Rovere, and Soatto 2017). In a two-sense version, the first sense crowded out the later one under joint training, and training each sense separately before fusing gave the best per-sense encoders, consistent with critical periods for multisensory integration (Kleinman, Achille, and Soatto 2023) and with accounts of limited early input (Turkewitz and Kenny 1982). In a cross-sense study with violations applied to a latent world, memory was the only architectural requirement shared by all senses, and perceptual narrowing emerged without being built in.

Discussion

So, do AI models learn like humans? Sometimes. Table 3 lists the signatures we tested. Given infant-like input, small predictive world models reproduce the order of sensory maturation (by construction), a critical period, perceptual narrowing, the advantage of combining senses under occlusion, and a benefit of early degraded input in hearing. They do not reproduce expectations about hidden objects, and network growth, often proposed as the computational analogue of brain development, only slows them down.

Table 3 | Which infant signatures appear, and why.
Infant signature Present in our models? What produces it
Body senses first, vision last Yes, by construction Front-end tables
Slow early vision Yes, beyond what the input requires Input plus slow extraction by a predictive objective
Early immaturity helps later In hearing (clean input), not in vision Degraded input as augmentation
Critical period for early deprivation Yes (companion study) Continuous training; no plasticity schedule needed
Perceptual narrowing Yes in vision, partly in hearing (companion study) Training statistics
Multisensory advantage under occlusion Yes Fusion of frozen sense latents
Object permanence (surprise at vanishing) No Not produced by squared-error prediction
Growth as development No: slower, half the compute Zero-gradient start of new units

What carries age. Three independent synthetic settings agree that the infant-like shape of development comes from the input schedule, and that growing the network mostly slows learning. This fits neurobiology, in which neurons are not added after birth but the periphery, synapse density, myelination and plasticity change on per-sense clocks (Huttenlocher and Dabholkar 1997; Sydnor et al. 2021; Hensch 2005). Capacity should be a controlled factor, not the definition of age, and age is best represented as experience: checkpoints of one continuous run, not separate models per age, because only a continuous run can show history effects such as critical periods.

What the constraints buy. The costs and benefits are specific and modest. Immature early vision costs a little on clean input and buys no robustness we can establish; immature early hearing improves clean localisation. This is the honest form of “starting small” (Elman 1993; Rohde and Plaut 1999): it is neither a free lunch nor a myth, and a full study must report both sides for every sense.

Why expectations need more than prediction. The failure of permanence is the most instructive result. The information is in the latent, yet the forecast does not use it, because a squared-error forecaster of pixels is rewarded for hedging. Objectives that predict in latent space (Garrido et al. 2025), represent uncertainty explicitly, or are trained on longer horizons should be tested against the same dissociating events.

Limitations. Everything is synthetic and small (at most 0.6 million parameters per sense) and evaluated mainly with linear probes, which measure decodability rather than behaviour. Hearing, touch and proprioception tables are placeholders, and “months” are training stages, not hours of experience. With 3 seeds per regime, several comparisons have large effect sizes but are not significant (Fig. 3c); we report them as estimates. An internal referee report and our responses are provided with the code (report/PEER_REVIEW.md).

Future work. Extending the study will use experience-matched checkpoints of one continuous run per sense, sensory-immaturity and plasticity schedules as the main levers with capacity as an ablation, late fusion with sense-onset order as a factor, infant paradigms (violation of expectation, habituation, preferential looking) as the primary read-outs, and perceptual narrowing as the flagship cross-sense test. The data path runs from this synthetic nursery to an embodied infant simulator for touch and proprioception (Mattern et al. 2024) and to headcam corpora for vision and hearing (Sullivan et al. 2021; Long et al. 2024).

Box 1 | Three perspectives on the same results

Mathematics.

Front ends bound what can be learned. Let YY be a property of the scene (the toy’s position) and Õa=Φs(O;a)\tilde O_a=\Phi_s(O;a) the filtered observation. For any learned representation Z=e(Õa)Z=e(\tilde O_a), the data-processing inequality gives I(Z;Y)≤I(Õa;Y)≤I(O;Y).I(Z;Y)\le I(\tilde O_a;Y)\le I(O;Y). The supervised ceiling in Fig. 2 estimates the middle term. The gap between ceiling and model is a property of learning; the ceiling itself is a property of the input.

Why a squared-error forecaster is not surprised. The minimiser of 𝔼∥ôt+1−ot+1∥2\mathbb E\lVert \hat o_{t+1}-o_{t+1}\rVert^2 over predictors of the past is the conditional mean ôt+1⋆=𝔼[ot+1∣o≤t]\hat o_{t+1}^\star=\mathbb E[o_{t+1}\mid o_{\le t}]. Behind a screen, let the toy reappear at frame t+1t+1 with probability pp. Then at each pixel the optimal forecast is a blend ô=(1−p)oscreen+potoy\hat o=(1-p)\,o^{\text{screen}}+p\,o^{\text{toy}}, and the expected surprise is Sreappear=(1−p)2Δ2,Svanish=p2Δ2,Δ=otoy−oscreen,S_{\text{reappear}}=(1-p)^2\Delta^2,\qquad S_{\text{vanish}}=p^2\Delta^2,\qquad \Delta=o^{\text{toy}}-o^{\text{screen}}, so a model is more surprised by reappearance whenever p<12p<\tfrac12, which holds for most frames of an occlusion of uncertain length. A negative VoE index is the expected behaviour of a well-trained pixel forecaster, not a failure of training.

Function-preserving growth and its delay. Widen a layer from nn to n′n' units, W1′=[W1R]W_1'=\begin{bmatrix}W_1\\R\end{bmatrix}, W2′=[W20]W_2'=[\,W_2\;\;0\,]. Then W2′ϕ(W1′x)=W2ϕ(W1x)W_2'\phi(W_1'x)=W_2\phi(W_1x) for every xx. The gradient on the new incoming weights is ∂ℒ∂R=(𝟎⊤δ)⊙ϕ′(Rx)x⊤=0,\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial R}=\big(\mathbf 0^\top\,\delta\big)\odot\phi'(Rx)\,x^\top=0, so new units cannot learn until their outgoing weights move away from zero, which takes a number of updates that grows with the learning rate’s inverse. The grown models pay this cost three times.

Computer science. Immature input is a curriculum in the sense of continuation methods: optimise a smoothed objective first, then track its minimiser as the smoothing is removed. Our hearing result (shuffled ≈ ordered > adult) suggests that here the benefit is mostly augmentation. Growth trades accuracy for compute: at matched updates it costs about half the parameter-updates. Late fusion of separately trained senses avoids the competition between modalities seen under joint training, a known problem in multimodal learning, and modality dropout trains cross-modal fill-in.

Neuroscience. Each front end stands for a peripheral or early stage that matures on its own clock: the optics and cone mosaic of the eye and the immature visual cortex (acuity, contrast, colour) (Banks and Bennett 1988); the cochlea and binaural brainstem circuits (frequency resolution, high-frequency sensitivity, interaural differences); the shrinking receptive fields of the skin and somatosensory cortex; and muscle-spindle and joint signals for proprioception. The memory window stands for working memory and persistent activity; the fusion model for multisensory integration in the superior colliculus and superior temporal sulcus. The brain grows synapses and then prunes them (Huttenlocher and Dabholkar 1997) rather than adding neurons, and closes plasticity on per-sense schedules governed by excitatory-inhibitory balance (Hensch 2005). Our growth ablation is therefore a test of an engineering idea, not of biology; the biologically motivated levers are sensory immaturity and plasticity schedules. Predictive coding frames all of this: each world model minimises the error of its own predictions, and violation-of-expectation is the behavioural read-out of that error.

Materials and Methods

Experimental design

The study compares six training regimes (Table 2) for four sense-specific world models at four checkpoints, with five analyses specified before the final runs: probes at adult-quality, own-age and newborn-quality input; a supervised information ceiling; violation-of-expectation surprise with dissociating events; occluded tracking and fill-in with a fusion model; and planned statistical comparisons (Table 4). Each regime is trained with the same data, the same number of updates and shared hyperparameters.

Environment

Episodes last T=20T=20 frames. A toy of type c∈{1,…,4}c\in\{1,\dots,4\} moves with constant velocity and bounces in a 32×32 scene; the hand’s position follows a smoothed random motor command ut∈ℝ2u_t\in\mathbb R^2 and stays in the lower half. Half the episodes contain a vertical screen. Vision is an RGB image on a dark background; the toy is drawn with a type-specific shape and colour, the screen in grey and the hand in skin tone. Hearing is a binaural spectrum, otaud∈ℝ2×32o^{\text{aud}}_t\in\mathbb R^{2\times32}, a Gaussian bump at a type-specific pitch whose loudness falls with distance and whose left/right balance follows horizontal position; sound passes through the screen. Touch is an 8×8 image of the toy’s shape when the hand overlaps the toy, otherwise zero. Proprioception is the hand’s normalised position and velocity. Ground truth includes toy position, type, visibility and contact. Training sets have 3,000 episodes per seed, test sets 400.

Probe events. Possible: the toy crosses a central screen horizontally and reappears. Impossible: the toy vanishes while hidden, from every sense. Vanish-visual: it vanishes from vision and touch but keeps sounding as if still moving. Silent: possible and impossible events with no sound at all (hearing receives noise only). Track: like possible, with a wider screen (14 px) and varied speed, so the toy is hidden for about seven frames. Paired events share random draws so that they differ only in the manipulation.

Growth. grow(w', k') widens every hidden layer as in Box 1 and lengthens the window by adding input weights of zero for the new (older) memory slots, so the model’s function is unchanged (verified for every layer by a unit test, tests/test_growth.py). Vision models grow from 43,507 to 586,499 parameters and hearing models from 13,792 to 149,088.

Training. Adam, learning rate 2×10−32\times10^{-3}, batch 32, 2,000 updates per stage for vision and 1,500 for other senses, four stages in one continuous run; weights carry over between stages and a fresh Adam optimiser is started at each stage, so all regimes see the same optimiser schedule. Hyperparameters were set once on the immature-input regime and shared by all regimes. Seeds: 3 for each regime (fusion uses the grown regime’s checkpoints).

Read-outs

Linear probes. For features XX (a latent, or a memory window of latents) and targets YY, ridge regression with centred targets and an unpenalised intercept, B̂=argminB∥(Y−Y‾)−XcB∥2+λ∥B∥2=(Xc⊤Xc+λI)−1Xc⊤(Y−Y‾),\hat B=\arg\min_B\lVert (Y-\bar Y)-X_cB\rVert^2+\lambda\lVert B\rVert^2=(X_c^\top X_c+\lambda I)^{-1}X_c^\top(Y-\bar Y), with XcX_c standardised features, is fitted on training episodes and evaluated on test episodes, R2=1−∑∥y−ŷ∥2/∑∥y−y‾∥2R^2=1-\sum\lVert y-\hat y\rVert^2/\sum\lVert y-\bar y\rVert^2. Adult-input probes use adult-quality input; own-age probes use the input quality of the checkpoint’s age; newborn-input probes are fitted on adult-quality input and tested on newborn-quality input.

Information ceiling. For each sense and age a∈{0,1,2,3,4,6,9,12}a\in\{0,1,2,3,4,6,9,12\}, a supervised network (the same encoder family) is trained for 1,500 updates to predict toy position and identity from a single filtered frame, and evaluated on held-out frames.

Violation of expectation. Surprise is one-step prediction error, St=∥d(ẑt)−õt∥2S_t=\lVert d(\hat z_t)-\tilde o_t\rVert^2 (unimodal) or ∥rs(ĥt)−zts∥2\lVert r_s(\hat h_t)-z^s_t\rVert^2 per channel (fused, standardised latents), averaged over the hidden stretch and the two frames after expected re-emergence. With SposS_{\text{pos}} and SimpS_{\text{imp}} the mean surprise on paired possible and impossible events, VoE=Simp−SposSimp+Spos,dz=Simp−Spos¯sd(Simp−Spos).\mathrm{VoE}=\frac{S_{\text{imp}}-S_{\text{pos}}}{S_{\text{imp}}+S_{\text{pos}}},\qquad d_z=\frac{\overline{S_{\text{imp}}-S_{\text{pos}}}}{\mathrm{sd}(S_{\text{imp}}-S_{\text{pos}})}.

Occluded tracking and fill-in. The hidden toy’s horizontal position is probed on fully hidden frames of the track events from the vision model’s memory window (k=6k=6 latents), from the hearing latent, and from the fused state, fitting on half of the episodes and testing on the other half. Fill-in probes toy position from the fused state with all senses, without vision, and from single senses.

Statistics. Bands and whiskers are ±1 s.d. over seeds. Planned comparisons at the 12-month checkpoint use Welch’s t-test and Hedges’ g=a‾−b‾sp(1−34(na+nb)−9)g=\frac{\bar a-\bar b}{s_p}\big(1-\frac{3}{4(n_a+n_b)-9}\big) with approximate 95% interval g±1.96na+nbnanb+g22(na+nb)g\pm1.96\sqrt{\frac{n_a+n_b}{n_an_b}+\frac{g^2}{2(n_a+n_b)}}; per-cell 95% bootstrap intervals are in results/extra.json. No correction for multiple comparisons is applied; we list all planned comparisons.

Compute. Training compute is approximated by ∑stages(parameters)×(updates)\sum_{\text{stages}}(\text{parameters})\times(\text{updates}); relative to a fixed 12-month-size network, grown vision models use 0.48 and grown hearing models 0.49.

Milestones. For each sense, the half-ceiling age is the first age at which the ceiling reaches half of its 12-month value (position R² for vision and hearing; identity accuracy above chance for touch). Kendall’s τ compares the resulting order with the order of functional maturity usually described for the three senses, touch before hearing before vision (Turkewitz and Kenny 1982).

Human and animal studies. The study uses only synthetic data; no human or animal participants were involved.

Code and data availability. All code, configurations and results are at github.com/pikulsomesh/developmental-world-models (MIT licence). scripts/run_experiments.py trains every regime, scripts/analyze_fusion_voe.py and scripts/analyze_extra.py run the analyses, scripts/make_paper_figures.py draws the figures, and scripts/fill_report.py writes every number in this report from the results files. An interactive companion is at pikulsomesh.github.io/developmental-world-models. Companion studies are in the project’s shared folder (research/age-modeling, research/cross-sense).
